chapter_summary:
After all the hard work of development, optimization, and debugging, the final step is to turn your Unity project into a playable game that can be distributed to players. This involves building your project for a specific platform and then deploying it. Unity's **Build Settings** (`File > Build Settings`) window is your central hub for this process.

First, you need to select your target platform. Unity supports a wide array of platforms, including PC (Windows, Mac, Linux), iOS, Android, WebGL, and various consoles. In the Build Settings window, you'll see a list of platforms. Select the one you want to build for and click "Switch Platform" if it's not already active. This process might take some time as Unity re-imports assets for the new platform.

Once the platform is selected, you'll configure the **Player Settings**. Click the "Player Settings..." button in the Build Settings window to open the Project Settings window to the "Player" section. This is where you customize crucial aspects of your game's identity and behavior on the target platform:
*   **Company Name & Product Name:** These define the application's identity.
*   **Version:** Important for updates and tracking.
*   **Icon:** Set the icon that will appear on the desktop or device home screen.
*   **Resolution and Presentation:** Control screen resolution, full-screen modes, and whether the game can be resized.
*   **Splash Screen:** Customize the Unity splash screen or add your own.
*   **Other Settings:** This section contains platform-specific settings. For example, on Android, you'll configure the bundle identifier, minimum API level, and keystore for signing. On iOS, you'll set the bundle identifier and signing team. These settings are critical for successful deployment to app stores.
*   **Scripting Backend:** For mobile platforms, you might choose IL2CPP over Mono for better performance and compatibility.
*   **API Compatibility Level:** Determines which .NET API subset your scripts can use.

A crucial distinction to make is between **Development Builds** and **Release Builds**. In the Build Settings window, you'll see checkboxes for "Development Build," "Script Debugging," and "Autoconnect Profiler."
*   **Development Build:** Includes debugging symbols, Unity's profiler, and usually the Unity splash screen. It's larger and slower but essential for testing and debugging on target devices.
*   **Script Debugging:** Allows you to attach an external debugger (like Visual Studio or Rider) to a running build on a device.
*   **Autoconnect Profiler:** Automatically connects the Unity Profiler in the editor to the running build, allowing you to profile performance on the device.
*   **Release Build:** This is your final, optimized game. It's smaller, faster, and does not include debugging tools. Always build a release version for distribution.

Once your Build Settings and Player Settings are configured, click the "Build" button. You'll be prompted to choose a destination folder for your build. Unity will then compile your scripts, process your assets, and package everything into an executable file (e.g., `.exe` for Windows, `.app` for Mac) or a platform-specific package (e.g., `.apk` for Android, `.ipa` for iOS, `.html` for WebGL).

**Common Build Errors and Warnings:**
*   **Script Errors:** If your project has compilation errors in your C# scripts, the build will fail. Resolve all errors in the Console before attempting to build.
*   **Missing References:** Assets or components referenced in your scene or scripts might be missing. Check the Console for "MissingReferenceException" or similar warnings.
*   **Platform-Specific Issues:** Some code or assets might not be compatible with your target platform. For instance, certain native plugins might only work on PC. Use `#if UNITY_ANDROID` preprocessor directives to conditionally compile code for specific platforms.
*   **Player Settings Misconfiguration:** Incorrect bundle identifiers, missing keystores (Android), or signing certificates (iOS) are common causes of build failures or deployment issues to app stores.

After a successful build, it's critical to **test your deployed build** on the actual target platform. The Unity Editor's Play Mode is a simulation and may not perfectly reflect real-world performance or behavior. Test on multiple devices if possible, especially those with lower specifications, to ensure a consistent experience. This is where remote debugging and profiling (as discussed in previous chapters) become invaluable.

```csharp
// Example of platform-specific code using preprocessor directives
void Start()
{
    #if UNITY_STANDALONE_WIN
        Debug.Log("Running on Windows PC.");
    #elif UNITY_ANDROID
        Debug.Log("Running on Android device.");
    #elif UNITY_IOS
        Debug.Log("Running on iOS device.");
    #elif UNITY_WEBGL
        Debug.Log("Running in WebGL browser.");
    #else
        Debug.Log("Running on an unknown platform.");
    #endif
}
```

Building and deploying can sometimes feel like a hurdle, but with careful attention to settings and a systematic approach to resolving errors, you'll successfully get your game into the hands of players.

screens.title: Building & Deploying Unity Games
screens.subtitle: From Build Settings to a tested platform build

narration.text: This chapter closes the loop between development and players by showing how to turn your Unity project into a distributable build. You will learn what the Build Settings window does, how to choose and switch target platforms, and why Player Settings control the identity and runtime behavior of your game. We will explore the practical difference between Development and Release builds, how to sign and package mobile builds, and how to troubleshoot common build errors. A concrete example will guide you through creating a PC standalone build, setting the company and product name, choosing a windowed resolution, and producing an executable you can run outside the editor. You will also see when to use script debugging and the autoconnect profiler, and why those tools belong to testing—not public releases. By the end of this lesson you will be able to prepare a build, locate its output package, and run basic device testing. Think about which platform you want to target first, because switching makes Unity reimport assets; plan time for that step.

keyIdea.text: Build Settings and Player Settings convert your project into platform-specific outputs; testing on real devices is essential before release.

screens.title: Build Settings: the central hub
screens.subtitle: What Build Settings does and why you use it

narration.text: Build Settings is Unity's central hub for producing platform builds. It lists supported targets like PC, WebGL, Android, and iOS, and it controls the active target you will compile for. Switching the active platform triggers Unity to reimport assets so they match target import settings, which is why switching can take several minutes for large projects. Practically, you use Build Settings to select scenes included in the build, choose the active platform, and enable testing options such as Development Build, Script Debugging, and Autoconnect Profiler. A concrete scenario: when preparing a PC standalone, select "PC, Mac & Linux Standalone", ensure your scenes are listed and checked, and then click Switch Platform if needed. A common misconception is that builds are independent of scenes—if a scene isn't listed in Build Settings it won't be included in the executable. Key takeaway: always confirm scene list and target platform before clicking Build to avoid missing content or wasted build time. How will you verify the scene list before building? Build Settings: the central hub means build settings selects the target platform, scenes to include, and testing options before packaging a build.. In practical terms, what build settings does and why you use it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Switching Target Platforms
screens.subtitle: Why switching matters and how to do it safely

narration.text: Switching the active target platform is a deliberate step because Unity must reimport assets and apply platform-specific import settings. The process is simple: open Build Settings, select the desired platform, and click Switch Platform. But there are practical implications to consider. Asset importers may change compression, texture formats, or shader variants for mobile versus desktop, which can change file sizes and runtime behavior. A concrete workflow example: if you plan to test on Android after developing on PC, switch to Android, allow reimport to finish, then open Player Settings to confirm your Android bundle identifier and keystore. A common mistake is switching platforms and immediately building without checking Player Settings—this can produce an unsigned package or one with the wrong identifier. To be safe, after switching, review the Player Settings platform tab, confirm resolution settings, scripting backend, and any platform-specific plugins. Key takeaway: treat platform switches as checkpoints where you validate identity, signing, and compatibility before building. Switching Target Platforms means switching platform triggers asset reimports; always validate player settings and signing after switching.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Player Settings: Identity & Presentation
screens.subtitle: Company, Product, Version, Icon, and Splash

narration.text: Player Settings control the game's visible identity and how it presents on devices. Core fields include Company Name and Product Name, which determine the app's package metadata and how it appears in stores and on home screens. Version helps track updates and should be incremented when you publish. Icon settings determine the icon shown on devices and desktops, and the Splash Screen controls the initial branding shown at startup. A practical example: set Company to Cohortia and Product to MyOptimizedGame before building a PC standalone so the application shows the correct name. A common misconception is thinking these values only matter for stores — they also affect file names, folder structures, and how operating systems display your app. Key takeaway: consistently update identity fields and versioning as part of your release checklist to avoid confusion and failed updates on store platforms. Player Settings: Identity & Presentation means player settings set identity and presentation details that affect store metadata, icons, versioning, and initial splash behavior.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Misconception

screens.title: Platform-specific Player Settings
screens.subtitle: Keystore, bundle identifier, signing, and scripting backend

narration.text: Platform-specific sections inside Player Settings contain the publishing and runtime options you must set before releasing. On Android you will set the bundle identifier and configure a keystore for signing; without a keystore an Android build cannot be published. On iOS you must set the bundle identifier and signing team to produce a deployable package. Mobile platforms also require choosing a scripting backend—IL2CPP is commonly used instead of Mono for performance and compatibility. A P I compatibility level affects which. NET APIs your scripts can access, and incorrect choices can cause compile or runtime errors. A concrete example: for Android open Player Settings, expand the Android tab, go to Publishing Settings, and either create a keystore or browse to an existing one, then assign a key alias. A frequent error is leaving the keystore unset; Unity will report a missing keystore during the build. Key takeaway: set platform-specific publishing and signing values early in your release pipeline to avoid blocked builds. screens.title: Development Build vs Release Build
screens.subtitle: When to use each and common trade-offs

narration.text: Understanding the difference between Development and Release builds is critical for a disciplined release workflow. Development Builds include debugging symbols, allow script debugging, and can autoconnect the profiler, which helps you find performance and correctness issues on target devices. However, they are larger, slower, and may expose internal state or debug messages, so they are not suitable for public distribution. Release Builds are optimized, stripped of debugging information, and generally smaller and faster; they are the builds you should submit to stores. A concrete contrast: during device testing enable Development Build and Autoconnect Profiler to diagnose a frame-rate drop on mobile; when you are ready to publish, uncheck Development Build and produce a Release Build to deliver the optimized package to players. A common misconception is that Development Builds behave identically to Release Builds; some performance characteristics change because of profiling hooks and unstripped symbols. Key takeaway: use Development Builds while debugging and always switch to Release for distribution. Development Build vs Release Build means development builds for debugging and profiling; release builds for distribution and performance.. In practical terms, when to use each and common trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Comparison

Development Build
Includes debug symbols, script debugging, and profiler hooks for testing on devices.
Useful for diagnosing crashes and measuring performance on actual hardware.
Larger file size and slower runtime due to debugging overhead.
Not recommended for public distribution.
Pro tip
Enable Autoconnect Profiler only when you need live profiling to avoid accidental profiling overhead.
Release Build
Optimized and stripped of debug info; smaller and faster; intended for players and stores.
Use for final distribution and store submissions.
Test on release builds too; some issues only appear without debug hooks.
Misconception

screens.title: Running a Build and Locating Outputs
screens.subtitle: How Unity compiles and where output files appear

narration.text: Executing a build compiles scripts, processes assets, and writes a platform-specific package to a chosen destination. After configuring Build and Player Settings, click Build and choose an empty folder; Unity will then package everything into an executable or platform package. For PC this often produces an executable file and a data folder, for Android an APK, for iOS an Xcode project or. ipa, and for WebGL a folder with an index H T M L and data files. A concrete example: build a PC standalone and save to a folder called MyOptimizedGame_PC_Build — after completion you will find the executable and can run it outside the editor to confirm behavior. A common mistake is selecting an existing folder that contains prior builds, which can mix files and cause confusion; choose an empty folder or clean the target first. Key takeaway: always note the chosen destination and verify the expected file types after the build finishes, then run the executable or package on the target platform to validate the result. screens.title: Common Build Errors & Warnings
screens.subtitle: Diagnose script errors, missing references, and platform incompatibilities

narration.text: Build failures usually fall into a small set of causes you can methodically address. First, script compilation errors: if any C# script fails to compile, the build process stops. Always resolve Console errors before building. Second, missing references: assets or components referenced in scenes or scripts may be missing, producing exceptions or warnings like MissingReferenceException; inspect the Console and the scene hierarchy to find broken links. Third, platform-specific incompatibilities: some plugins or native code only work on certain platforms; use preprocessor directives to isolate platform code and avoid compilation errors on other targets. A concrete remediation example: if Android build fails due to a missing keystore, open Player Settings, go to the Android Publishing Settings, and create or set the keystore and key alias. A common misconception is that a successful Play Mode run guarantees a successful build—Play Mode uses the Editor environment which can mask missing platform-specific setup. Key takeaway: use the Console to fix compile errors, verify references, and validate platform-specific settings to achieve successful builds. Common Build Errors & Warnings means resolve compilation errors and missing references, and handle platform-specific code to avoid build failures.. In practical terms, diagnose script errors, missing references, and platform incompatibilities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Resolve compilation errors and missing references, and handle platform-specific code to avoid build failures.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.6 › Common Build Errors
Script Errors
Fix any Console compilation errors first. A single failing script prevents a build.
Use the Console to jump to the script and correct the error before building again.
Missing References
Inspect scenes and prefabs for broken links or missing assets that raise runtime exceptions.
Platform incompatibilities
Guard platform-specific code with preprocessor directives to avoid compilation issues on other targets.
Example fix
If a native plugin works only on PC, wrap calls in platform checks so mobile builds don't attempt to compile incompatible code.
Tip
Always re-run a build after fixing Console errors to confirm the build pipeline completes cleanly.

screens.title: Platform-Specific Directives
screens.subtitle: Use preprocessor checks to isolate platform code

narration.text: Preprocessor directives let you include or exclude code at compile time depending on the target platform. This prevents platform-specific APIs from causing compile errors on other targets. For example, wrapping a call in a directive that checks for Android ensures that code using Android-only APIs is not compiled for PC. A practical example from the chapter shows basic directives that log the active platform at startup. When you see #if UNITY_ANDROID or #elif UNITY_IOS, the compiler includes only the matching block for the selected platform. A common misconception is that these directives run at runtime—they are evaluated at compile time, so the non-matching blocks are removed from the build. To validate behavior, test builds on the intended target and use Development Build plus Script Debugging when diagnosing issues. Key takeaway: use preprocessor directives to keep platform-specific code isolated, and always test the resulting build on the target device. Platform-Specific Directives means use #if directives to compile platform-specific code only for matching build targets, preventing cross-platform compile errors.. In practical terms, use preprocessor checks to isolate platform code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Code pattern
keyIdea.text: Use #if directives to compile platform-specific code only for matching build targets, preventing cross-platform compile errors.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.6 › Platform-Specific Directives
What it is
Preprocessor directives conditionally include code at compile time based on the active platform.
// Example: platform-specific log on Start\nvoid Start()\n{\n #if UNITY_STANDALONE_WIN\n Debug.Log("Running on Windows PC.");\n #elif UNITY_ANDROID\n Debug.Log("Running on Android device.");\n #elif UNITY_IOS\n Debug.Log("Running on iOS device.");\n #elif UNITY_WEBGL\n Debug.Log("Running in WebGL browser.");\n #else\n Debug.Log("Running on an unknown platform.");\n #endif\n}
Key note
Directives are resolved at compile time; non-matching blocks are excluded from the final build.
Concrete example
If a plugin is PC-only, wrap its usage in a WINDOWS directive so mobile builds won't try to compile it and fail.
Misconception
They are not runtime conditionals; they change which code is compiled into the build itself.
Key Takeaway

Use preprocessor directives to protect platform-specific code and test on target hardware to confirm behavior.

screens.title: Testing Deployed Builds
screens.subtitle: Why editor play mode isn't enough and how to test on devices

narration.text: Testing your build on the actual target platform is essential because the Editor simulates but does not perfectly match device behavior. Differences can appear in performance, input handling, file paths, and plugin behavior. A practical testing routine: first build a Development Build and enable Script Debugging if you need to attach a debugger; this helps reproduce issues on device. Use Autoconnect Profiler to gather frame-time and memory information from the running build. Then run a Release build to verify performance without debug overhead. Test on multiple hardware profiles, especially lower-spec devices, to uncover performance regressions. For mobile, also test installation, permissions, and portrait versus landscape modes. A common misconception is that Play Mode timing equals device timing; profiling on the actual device often reveals different bottlenecks. Key takeaway: combine Development Builds for debugging with Release Builds for final performance verification and test across representative devices to ensure consistent behavior. Testing Deployed Builds means test on real devices using development builds for debugging and release builds for performance verification across hardware profiles.. In practical terms, why editor play mode isn't enough and how to test on devices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.6 › Testing Deployed Builds
Testing checklist
Build a Development Build and enable Script Debugging when you need to attach a debugger to the running app.
Use Autoconnect Profiler to capture device performance data during real runs.
Produce a Release Build to confirm performance without debug overhead.
Device testing notes
Test installation, resolution modes, permissions, and low-end hardware to ensure robustness.
Concrete example
Enable Autoconnect Profiler while running a Development Build on your phone to capture frame spikes and then fix the most costly draw calls or scripts.
Misconception
Passing Play Mode tests does not guarantee builds will run identically on devices; always test on the target hardware.

screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These are the essential concepts to keep in mind. Build Settings is the hub where you choose a target platform, list scenes to include, and enable test-time options; always verify scene inclusion. Player Settings control identity, resolution, icons, and all platform-specific publishing options like bundle identifiers and keystores; set them before building. Development Builds provide debugging tools and profiler connections useful during testing but are larger and not for distribution, while Release Builds are optimized for players. Finally, test your builds on the intended hardware because the Editor does not guarantee identical behavior. Use these ideas as a checklist during each release cycle to reduce errors and ensure a smooth deployment.
